_about: Reference list for flagging non-native and regulated plants in Maine. `watchlist` is what a survey should actively hunt for; `classification` is the status of species already in this guide.
_source: Compiled from Maine DACF's Do Not Sell list (Rule Chapter 192) and Advisory List. Checked against the published page on 2026-08-03, which carries additions effective 1/1/2024. Two entries below are NOT confirmed against that page and are left flagged deliberately — see _unconfirmed. VERIFY against the current published list, and against the printable PDF the page links, before reporting anything to an agency.

_status_values.introduced: Non-native and naturalized, but not regulated and not aggressively displacing natives.
_status_values.invasive: Non-native and known to displace native vegetation. Worth recording.
_status_values.regulated: On Maine's Do Not Sell list. A find here is reportable and may warrant treatment.
_status_values.unknown: Not determined — usually because the record is only identified to genus.

watchlist.why: Forms dense monocultures, destabilizes banks, extremely hard to remove once established. Very common on the Maine coast.
watchlist.look_for: Bamboo-like hollow stems to 10ft, heart/shovel-shaped leaves cut straight across the base, sprays of small white flowers late summer.

watchlist.why: Strangles and topples mature trees. Among the most damaging invasives in coastal Maine.
watchlist.look_for: Twining woody vine, round finely-toothed leaves, orange-yellow capsules splitting to red berries along the stem (native bittersweet fruits only at branch tips).

watchlist.why: Serious problem on Maine's coastal islands. Monarchs lay eggs on it and the larvae die.
watchlist.look_for: Twining vine, opposite glossy leaves, tiny dark purple star-shaped flowers, milkweed-like pods.

watchlist.why: Dominates wet edges and shades out regeneration.
watchlist.look_for: Shrub/small tree, glossy untoothed oval leaves with 8-9 strongly parallel vein pairs, berries ripening red to black.

watchlist.why: Alters soil chemistry and elevates tick densities.
watchlist.look_for: Low thorny shrub, small spoon-shaped leaves in clusters, single spine at each node, bright red oblong berries, yellow inner bark.

watchlist.why: Leafs out earliest in spring and shades the forest floor before natives start.
watchlist.look_for: Opposite untoothed oval leaves, HOLLOW older stems, paired red berries.

watchlist.why: Forms impenetrable thickets in old fields.
watchlist.look_for: Arching thorny canes, clusters of small white flowers, and the giveaway — fringed/comb-like stipules at the leaf base.

watchlist.why: Takes over wetlands and reduces waterfowl habitat value.
watchlist.look_for: Tall magenta flower spikes in wet ground, square stems, opposite or whorled stalkless leaves.

watchlist.why: Replaces salt marsh vegetation. Directly relevant to any island marsh edge.
watchlist.look_for: Reed to 15ft with a dense feathery plume. A native subspecies exists — the introduced one is taller, denser, with tighter plumes and ridged stems.

watchlist.why: Releases compounds that suppress the fungi tree seedlings depend on.
watchlist.look_for: Kidney-shaped scalloped basal leaves year one, 2-3ft stalk with small 4-petal white flowers year two. Crushed leaves smell of garlic.

watchlist.why: Dense shade and shallow roots prevent native regeneration beneath it.
watchlist.look_for: Maple-shaped leaves wider than long; snap a leaf stalk — milky white sap confirms it.

watchlist.why: Fixes nitrogen and changes soil chemistry; bird-spread.
watchlist.look_for: Shrub with leaves distinctly SILVERY-scaly underneath, speckled red berries.

watchlist.why: Escapes from plantings into forest understory.
watchlist.look_for: Corky wings running down the twigs; brilliant red fall color.

watchlist.why: Same impacts as glossy buckthorn, drier sites.
watchlist.look_for: Sub-opposite toothed leaves with curving veins, twigs often ending in a short thorn.

watchlist.why: Forms dense mats in wetlands and displaces native marsh plants.
watchlist.look_for: Yellow flag iris in standing water; sword-shaped leaves.

broadleaf-plantain.note: European; naturalized in disturbed ground everywhere. Not regulated.

dandelion.note: European; ubiquitous, not considered ecologically damaging.

yarrow.note: Achillea millefolium is a complex — Maine has both a native subspecies and introduced European forms, not separable from a photo.

queen-annes-lace.note: European. Listed as invasive in several states but not regulated in Maine; aggressive in old fields.

common-ragweed.note: Native despite its reputation — the allergy is real, the plant belongs here.

self-heal.note: Native and European subspecies both occur; not separable from a photo.

st-johns-wort.note: European. A serious rangeland invasive in the western US; naturalized without major impact in Maine.

coltsfoot.note: European. Added to Maine's Do Not Sell list effective 1/1/2024 — this entry previously said it was not listed. Colonizes disturbed gravel and streambanks in dense mats.

lupine.note: Worth knowing: the iconic roadside lupine is NOT native to Maine — it is a western North American species. It displaces native meadow flora and hybridizes with the rare native sundial lupine.

vetch.note: Genus only. Vicia includes native and introduced species; V. cracca is a common introduced one.

wild-rose.note: PRIORITY RECHECK — if this is Rosa multiflora it is regulated. Check for fringed comb-like stipules at the leaf base.

rubus.note: Genus only; most Maine Rubus is native, but Rubus phoenicolasius (wineberry) was added to the Do Not Sell list 1/1/2024. Check for dense red bristly hairs on the canes.

mountain-ash.note: Sorbus americana is native. The European S. aucuparia was added to the Do Not Sell list 1/1/2024; it has hairier winter buds and duller leaves.

eastern-hemlock.note: Native and under threat itself — hemlock woolly adelgid is established in coastal Maine. Worth recording stand health.

gray-dogwood.note: Genus only, but all Maine Cornus shrubs are native.

bush-honeysuckle-invasive.note: On Maine's Do Not Sell list. Confirmed in this dataset.

pipsissewa.note: Native and slow-spreading; locally uncommon. Presence is a good sign for site quality.

smooth-bedstraw.note: European. A significant agricultural pest in Maine hayfields; forms dense mats.

willowherb.note: Genus only; Epilobium includes native and introduced species.

wild-lettuce.note: Genus only; L. canadensis is native, L. serriola is introduced.

buttercup.note: Ranunculus acris is European and common in pasture. Note R. repens (creeping buttercup) was added to the Do Not Sell list 1/1/2024 — it creeps by runners and has a paler blotch on the leaves.

hay-scented-fern.note: Native but aggressively colonial — dense stands suppress tree regeneration, so worth mapping even though it belongs here.

ash-sapling.note: Native and under threat — emerald ash borer is in Maine. Ash locations are worth recording for monitoring.

_unconfirmed.note: Marked regulated here; did not appear in the 2026-08-03 reading of the DACF page. Left as regulated on purpose — over-flagging a genuine invasive costs a walk, under-flagging misses an infestation. Confirm against the printable PDF.
Same. The page lists Frangula alnus (glossy buckthorn) but common buckthorn was not seen. Confirm before relying on the status.
